title: The Same Page (andrewmarcinek.substack.com), September 1, 2026
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek argues that the current parental backlash against school technology (the 'techlash') is less about the devices themselves than about a decade of one-directional communication: schools rolled out laptops and tablets with signature forms instead of explanations. He synthesizes research from the American Academy of Pediatrics, NAEYC/Fred Rogers Center, Hirsh-Pasek's four-question framework for educational media, UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report, and Karen Mapp's family-engagement scholarship to argue that the school is uniquely positioned to model good tech use because it has the tool, the task, and the teacher in the same room as the child. He warns against the reactive instinct to appease vocal parents by banning devices outright, arguing this mistakes a symptom (families were never included) for the whole disease. In response, he releases a concrete framework, 'The Same Page,' built around five family touch points embedded in events schools already run: a Family Brief, a back-to-school-night task, a conference template, a winter joint-tech session, and a spring listening session. The piece closes with his central formulation: restriction without instruction is incomplete policy, and policy without conversation is incomplete too.
points: Argues the techlash is largely a communication failure: devices arrived home with a signature form, not an explanation of purpose.
Synthesizes AAP, NAEYC/Fred Rogers Center, Hirsh-Pasek, UNESCO, and Karen Mapp research into one throughline: what matters is the adult alongside the screen, not the device itself.
Warns against reactive appeasement—banning devices to quiet a few vocal parents—as treating a legitimate complaint (exclusion from the conversation) as the entire problem.

Introduces 'The Same Page,' a free five-touch-point framework (Family Brief, back-to-school night task, conference template, winter joint-media session, spring listening session) built into events schools already run.
Frames the goal as shared authorship of meaning between school and home: one child, two sets of adults, one coherent story about what the screen is for.
quotes: I have been on the school side of more than one device rollout, and I can tell you exactly what most families received about it. A form.

We were proud of the rollout. We had thought hard about the pedagogy, or believed we had. What we had not thought about was the kitchen table, where a parent was looking at a Chromebook with no idea what it was for.
Devices arrived faster than pedagogy changed. Vendors outran evidence. But underneath all of it, schools went into the deep end on edtech and did not adequately bring families with them.
Those parents are telling you something true, that they were never brought into the conversation. The fix for that is not to let a few of them write the program from the parking lot.
It has the tool, the task, and the teacher in one room. No other institution in a child's life does.
Read that list against the backpack form and you can see every place we went wrong.
Restriction without instruction is incomplete policy, and I'd add that policy without conversation is incomplete too. Start the conversation. Then keep it going.
